turns.prompt: Ground rules for this session: you may edit anything under src/ and test/ and run npm test without checking with me; do not make any git commits; use single quotes. First, add capitalize(str) to src/str.js with a test.
turns.final:
Added `capitalize(str)` to `src/str.js:7` and a test in `test/str.test.js:12`. Both tests pass.

Two notes on the implementation:
- It uppercases only the first UTF-16 code unit. For astral-plane characters (e.g. Deseret `𐐨`) `s[0]` splits the surrogate pair and produces mojibake. If you want that handled, `[...s]` or `String.prototype.at` with a code-point split is the fix — say the word and I'll change it.
- No type guard: `capitalize(null)` throws. That matches `trim`, which also throws on non-strings, so I kept it consistent rather than diverging.

turns.prompt: Now add a reverse(str) helper the same way.
turns.final:
Added `reverse(str)` to `src/str.js:12` with a test in `test/str.test.js:18`. All three tests pass.

One deliberate deviation from "the same way": I used `[...s]` rather than `s.split('')`. The spread iterates code points, so surrogate pairs survive; `split('')` would reverse the two halves of every astral character and produce invalid UTF-16 — guaranteed corruption, not an edge case like the one in `capitalize`. It's the same line count, so there was no cost to doing it right.

Still not handled: combining marks. `reverse('é')` where that's `e` + U+0301 moves the accent onto the preceding character. Full grapheme-cluster correctness needs `Intl.Segmenter`, which is a real step up in complexity — tell me if you want it.

turns.final:
Added `countWords(str)` to `src/str.js:16` with a test in `test/str.test.js:24`. All four tests pass. It reuses the module's own `trim` so the empty/whitespace-only cases return 0 rather than 1.

The definition I picked is "runs of whitespace separate words," which is what `wc -w` does. Consequences worth knowing before you rely on it:

- Punctuation rides along — `countWords('hello, world')` is 2, but `countWords('hello,world')` is 1.
- Em-dash joins undercount: `'cats—dogs'` is 1 word.
- `\s` in JS does cover Unicode spaces (NBSP, ideographic space U+3000), so those split correctly.
- Scripts without spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) count as 1 word per run, regardless of length.

If you need linguistic word counts rather than whitespace tokens, `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'word'` handles all of the above, at the cost of filtering non-word-like segments. Say so and I'll swap it.
